name: Classical Greek hoplite warfare

weightNotes.aggression: Hanson (Western Way of War): invaders ravaged farmland to force a short, decisive pitched battle, which defenders usually accepted. Above mid, not higher because many campaigns ended in ravaging without battle.
weightNotes.maneuver: Two phalanxes met head-on on level ground; the decision came by collision and shoving (othismos). Near-pure attrition.
weightNotes.flanking: Flanking was mostly incidental: the rightward drift of lines (Mantinea 418) let the strong right wing overlap. Deliberate schemes (Leuctra 371, Theban column at least fifty shields deep) were late exceptions.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Poor at assault; cities fell by blockade or betrayal over months or years (Potidaea, Plataea 429-427). Armies preferred ravaging to provoke battle.
weightNotes.reserveUse: The whole phalanx was committed at once; held-back reserves are nearly absent before the 4th century.
weightNotes.scouting: Little cavalry in most poleis; Sparta's mora was caught in the open by peltasts at Lechaeum (390). Low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Krentz (GRBS 1985): defeated hoplite armies typically lost 10-20% killed (average about 14%, including the pursuit), victors about 5%. The break therefore came at well under 10% loss; 0.08.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Hoplites decided battles; psiloi, archers and cavalry were marginal until peltasts and cavalry grew in the 4th century (Lechaeum, Sphacteria).
weightNotes.initiative: Sparta's layered officer chain gave tactical responsiveness; most poleis were citizen militias with elected generals and little drill. Weighted average 0.3.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Short-range, short-season campaigns: citizens brought a few days' rations and relied on markets and plunder, so operations stayed near home and ended when food or the season ran out.

summary: Citizen heavy infantry (hoplites with large round shield, spear and bronze armour) fought in a close-order phalanx usually eight deep. Campaigns were short summer invasions of a neighbour's farmland intended to provoke a single pitched battle on level ground, decided within hours by collision and push; the victor held the field and set up a trophy, and pursuit was limited. Light troops, cavalry and sieges were secondary; Sparta was the professional exception within the same system.
whyItWorked: The phalanx was very hard to break frontally on open ground, and heavily armoured hoplites outclassed lightly protected missile infantry at close quarters, as at Marathon and Plataea. The system matched the economics of farmer-citizen states: short, decisive and cheap.
whereItFailed: On broken ground or against light troops who refused contact: Sphacteria (425), where Spartans were worn down by archers and psiloi and the survivors surrendered; Lechaeum (390), where Iphicrates's peltasts killed about 250 of a 600-man Spartan mora with minimal losses. Against a concentrated, deep attack on one point: Leuctra (371). In long wars, its inability to take cities or campaign out of season made the Peloponnesian War a war of blockades and fleets.

sources.title: Krentz, Casualties in Hoplite Battles, GRBS 26 (1985)
Hanson, The Western Way of War (2nd ed. 2000)
